name: Catalpa
lede: Catalpa is a pale purple from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, far more common in Claude Monet's paintings than anywhere else in our archive.

sections.title: A dictionary name, 1892
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color dates the name to 1892, at plate 44, column D, chip 3, hex #A38F9B [1]. No Ridgway or ISCC-NBS plate is recorded for it independently in this library; the ISCC-NBS committee's 1955 match places it among the "grayish purple" names, 3.9 units away [1]. Its Munsell notation is 1.3RP 6.0/2.7 [1]. The catalpa tree carries pale, purple-spotted flowers, but the dictionary entry consulted here does not explain the name, so the link stays an open question rather than a claim [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[pastel-violet|Pastel Violet]], about three units away [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of Catalpa covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 63 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.3 per cent, as photographed [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1910s, and Claude Monet carries it nearly thirty-eight times the archive average, far more than any other painter; John Singer Sargent follows well behind [2]. Its earliest appearance is a 1405 altarpiece, *Saint Dominic Guzmán and Four Saints* [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [2].

origin.named_after: undocumented (name also carried by the catalpa tree, whose flowers are pale and purple-spotted)
